beats.lead: The oldest surviving photograph does not have a firm date.
beats.text: Nicéphore Niépce made it sometime between 1822 and 1827, using a process he called heliography, meaning sun-drawing.
beats.note: Historians narrowed the window from his letters to his brother; nobody has pinned it closer than that.

beats.text: The popular version says the exposure took eight hours. That number is a mid-twentieth-century guess, based only on how sunlight falls on both sides of the buildings in the image.
beats.note: A researcher who rebuilt Niépce's process using historically accurate materials found it actually needed several days of exposure, not hours.

beats.name: Helmut and Alison Gernsheim
beats.role: photography historians who tracked down Niépce's photograph after it had effectively vanished from view earlier in the twentieth century.

beats.text: Niépce partnered with Louis Daguerre in 1829. After Niépce died in 1833, Daguerre kept working alone and unveiled his own process a decade later, naming it after himself.
beats.note: The French government paid Daguerre 6,000 francs a year for it. Niépce's own estate received only 4,000.

beats.text: The man who actually took photography's first surviving picture died broke. His grave was paid for by his town.

beats.line: Photography's first surviving picture spent decades forgotten before anyone came looking.
